title: Advanced Subclinical Atherosclerosis in Young Individuals and Risk of Mortality Over 30 Years: The Coronary Artery Calcium Consortium
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring is a well-established tool for predicting cardiovascular risk, but its long-term prognostic value in young adults remains unclear. As early preventive intervention may yield substantial lifetime benefit, understanding long-term implications of elevated CAC in young adults is important for informing prevention strategies. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the long-term risk of all-cause, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and coronary heart disease (CHD) mortality associated with premature advanced subclinical atherosclerosis. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study used the CAC Consortium dataset, a retrospectively assembled cohort of referred individuals with clinically indicated CAC scans. Using multivariable regression models for time-to-event analysis, the association of CAC with all-cause, CVD, and CHD mortality was assessed, adjusting for age, sex, and traditional atherosclerotic CVD risk factors. Cumulative incidence was derived for these outcomes in 5-year increments up to 30 years using a mixed approach involving the Kaplan-Meier method and Weibull modeling. The proportion of deaths attributable to CVD and CHD across CAC groups was evaluated. Four institutions across the US provided patient-level data to assemble the CAC Consortium. Included in the analysis were adults aged 30 to 45 years from the CAC Consortium. They were followed up for a median of 22.6 years. Study data were analyzed from October 2025 to September 2026. EXPOSURE: Elevated CAC in adults aged 30 to 45 years, specifically CAC score greater than 90%. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Participants were followed up for underlying cause of mortality. RESULTS: Among 12 847 participants, the mean (SD) age was 40.5 (3.6) years, and 9922 (77.2%) were male; 9262 (72.1%) had CAC score of 0, 1626 (12.7%) had a CAC score between 75% to 90%, and 1703 (13.3%) had a CAC score greater than 90%. In total, there were 624 deaths (149 CVD and 81 CHD). Multivariable adjusted hazard ratios for CAC score greater than 90% vs CAC score of 0 were 1.87 (95% CI, 1.54-2.27), 2.60 (95% CI, 1.77-3.82), and 3.71 (95% CI, 2.24-6.16), for all-cause, CVD, and CHD mortality, respectively. Over 30 years, the group with a CAC score greater than 90% had significantly higher modeled risk of all-cause (12.9% vs 7.5%), CVD (4.5% vs 1.5%), and CHD (3.0% vs 0.6%) mortality, compared with the group with a CAC score of 0. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Results of this cohort study suggest that young adults with a CAC score greater than 90% face significantly higher long-term risk of all-cause, CVD, and CHD mortality, suggesting potential implications for guiding the intensification of preventive intervention in this high-risk phenotype.

title: Finerenone-Empagliflozin Combination Therapy in Apparent Resistant Hypertension: A CONFIDENCE Trial Post Hoc Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Apparent treatment-resistant hypertension (aTRH) is common in chronic kidney disease (CKD) with type 2 diabetes and predicts worse outcomes. Spironolactone, the established fourth-line agent, is limited by hyperkalemia in CKD. OBJECTIVES: This analysis assessed whether finerenone plus empagliflozin lowers blood pressure (BP) meaningfully in aTRH, and whether aTRH modifies these agents' efficacy and safety. METHODS: Post hoc analysis of CONFIDENCE (NCT05254002), a double-blind randomized trial of finerenone, empagliflozin, or both in CKD with albuminuria and type 2 diabetes. aTRH was BP ≥130/80 mm Hg on 3 antihypertensive drugs, or ≥4 drugs regardless of BP. Mixed models and logistic regression identified predictors of BP response. RESULTS: Of the 796 participants, 307 (39%) had aTRH; they were older, more obese, and had more atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, higher albuminuria, and higher systolic BP (140.9 vs 131.5 mm Hg) but similar estimated glomerular filtration rate (53 vs 55 mL/min/1.73 m2). Combination therapy lowered systolic BP more than either monotherapy. Independent predictors of a ≥10 mm Hg systolic BP fall were aTRH (OR: 1.56; 95% CI: 1.08-2.25) and higher baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (OR: 1.15 per 10 mL/min/1.73 m2; 95% CI: 1.05-1.26); diuretic use and albuminuria were not. The aTRH effect was treatment-independent (interaction P = 0.21). Adverse events were more frequent with aTRH (63.8% vs 51.1%), yet on combination therapy hyperkalemia was less frequent (11.2% vs 17.5%). CONCLUSIONS: aTRH affected approximately 40% of participants and marked a higher-risk phenotype responsive to finerenone-empagliflozin, with BP reductions comparable to spironolactone but without the excess hyperkalemia that limits its use in CKD.

title: Sex differences in cardiovascular disease burden, risk factors, and disease spectrum in Europe: a global burden of disease 2023 analysis within the ESC Atlas framework
abstract: Despite growing recognition of sex disparities in cardiovascular disease (CVD), contemporary, harmonized analyses of sex-specific burden in the European region that could inform targeted prevention strategies, remain limited. Sex-specific patterns in CVD burden and risk factor exposure across 55 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) member countries were examined using data from the 2023 Global Burden of Disease study. Risk factor exposure was quantified using age-sex-standardized summary exposure values for 10 established cardiovascular risk factors. Disease incidence and mortality for major CVD categories, including maternal hypertensive disorders, were estimated by calculating age-sex-standardized rates per 100 000 person-years using the 2013 European Standard Population. Analyses were performed by sex at country, regional, and ESC-wide levels and over time (1990-2023). In 2023, in the ESC region, the overall CVD burden was broadly similar in men and women, with women accounting for 55% (6.0 million) of cases and 50% of deaths (1.5 million). This apparent parity, however, concealed marked sex differences in disease composition, risk exposure, and geographic disparities. Compared with men, women had a lower proportion of CVD due to ischaemic heart disease (21% vs 38%) and a higher contribution from peripheral arterial disease (23% vs 19%). Major differences were also apparent in risk profiles, particularly for behavioural risk factors-with summary exposure values of tobacco and alcohol being 10%-20% points higher in men than women; contrasting with cardiometabolic factors, such as high body mass index and low physical activity, that were often 5%-15% points higher in women than men, and more modest differences in environmental and biological risks, including air pollution, fasting glucose, or cholesterol. Cardiovascular disease burden further varied widely across countries and disparities affected women more strongly than men, with an approximately three-fold difference between the lowest- and highest-incidence countries in women, compared with a two-fold difference in men, and even larger disparities in mortality and premature mortality (up to 25-fold in women). Maternal hypertensive disorders substantially shaped both the scale and composition of CVD burden in women, accounting for 25% of incident CVD in women and exhibiting substantial geographic variation, with up to 18-fold differences in incidence across countries. These findings challenge conventional approaches that treat CVD as a homogeneous condition. In particular, the substantial contribution of non-ischaemic conditions and maternal hypertensive disorders to the burden in women, alongside distinct patterns of risk exposure and wider geographic disparities, underscore the importance of adopting a life-course and sex- and gender-informed approach to cardiovascular prevention and policy.

title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: AIMS: Whether a retinal artificial intelligence (AI) risk score reclassifies SCORE2 cardiovascular risk stratification in statin-naive adults across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary is uncertain. We evaluated the retinal AI risk score for 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prediction. METHODS: In 40,672 statin-naive UK Biobank participants (aged 40-69, without diabetes), cardiovascular risk categories and treatment recommendation status (Class I or IIa vs neither) were defined using the 2025 ESC/EAS focused-update framework. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) adjusted for SCORE2 or for established risk factors. The incremental predictive value of adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. RESULTS: Over a 10.0-year median follow-up (914 ASCVD events), the very high retinal AI risk group independently predicted ASCVD (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.32 vs low risk; p<0.001). Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 reclassified risk across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary (statin-eligibility NRI [net reclassification improvement] 0.012, p<0.001); reclassification was statistically significant but modest (continuous NRI 0.445, p<0.001), without C-index or net-benefit gain. In the statin-indicated subgroup, retinal AI risk groups further stratified risk (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.16; p<0.001). Statin-not-indicated participants in the high or very high retinal AI risk groups had numerically similar observed 10-year risk to all statin-indicated, untreated participants (p=0.758). There was no evidence of effect modification by clinically detectable retinal disorder (interaction p=0.93). Incremental value was greater in women than men (sex interaction p<0.001). CONCLUSION: Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 produced modest bidirectional risk reclassification across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary; these findings warrant prospective validation.Abstract word count: 250 words.

title: Life-Course Blood Pressure Trajectories and Focal Myocardial Fibrosis in Older Age in MyoFit46
abstract: BACKGROUND: The impact of life-course blood pressure (BP) trajectories on later-life focal left ventricular (LV) fibrosis by late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) remains elusive. METHODS: MyoFit46 prospectively recruited ≈500 participants from a 1946 birth cohort for a cardiovascular magnetic resonance scan at 77 years, assessing LV LGE calculated using the 3-SD method or 5-SD method. Systolic BP (SBP) and diastolic BP were recorded at 36, 43, 53, 63, 69, and 77 years. For each participant, annual rates of BP change (steepness) and area under the BP trajectory (cumulative burden) for each age interval were calculated using mixed-effects models. Associations between life-course BPs and LGE were tested using generalized linear models, adjusted for antihypertensives, demographics, lifestyle, and comorbidities. Time-to-event associations between LGE and incident major adverse cardiovascular event (hospitalizations for coronary artery disease, stroke, heart failure, and atrial/ventricular arrhythmias; n=29) were also evaluated. RESULTS: Among 472 participants (54% male), each 10 mm Hg greater individual SBPs at 36 to 69 years were associated with 6% to 11% greater LV LGE calculated using the 3-SD method (all P≤0.033), whereas each 10 mm Hg sustained greater SBPs on any age interval from 36 to 69 associated with 16% to 24% greater LGE calculated using the 3-SD method at 77(all P≤0.005), independent of SBP at 77 years. Each 1 mm Hg/y steeper SBP rise during age intervals 36 to 43, 43 to 53, and 53 to 63 was associated with 6% to 12% greater LGE calculated using the 3-SD method at 77 years. LGE presence was associated with greater major adverse cardiovascular event rates (hazard ratio, 2.5 [95% CI, 1.2-5.2]). CONCLUSIONS: Higher life-course BPs, cumulative burden, and steeper increases were associated with greater older-age LV LGE, which was linked to incident major adverse cardiovascular events. BP trajectories, beyond single-point BP measurements, warrant further investigation as tools to guide BP management strategies.

title: Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea
abstract: BACKGROUND: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). METHODS: In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results. RESULTS: A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. CONCLUSIONS: In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).

title: Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitor Use and Levels of Hemoglobin, Markers of Iron Metabolism, and Erythropoiesis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
abstract: IMPORTANCE: In randomized clinical trials, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor use was associated with increased hemoglobin and hematocrit compared with placebo. However, the magnitude and importance of this association remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the associations between SGLT2 inhibitor use and levels of hemoglobin, hematocrit, and markers of iron metabolism and erythropoiesis compared with placebo or active comparator. DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched from inception to July 22, 2026. STUDY SELECTION: Randomized, double-masked clinical trials comparing SGLT2 inhibitor use with placebo or active comparators in patients with 1 or more of the following conditions: cardiovascular disease, diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease. DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Three reviewers independently extracted data and results were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcomes were changes in hemoglobin and hematocrit. Secondary outcomes were changes in red blood cell concentration, erythropoietin (EPO), and iron measures (serum iron, ferritin, transferrin saturation, and hepcidin). RESULTS: A total of 85 randomized clinical trials were analyzed (median [IQR] duration, 24 [12-32] weeks), including 70 543 participants (mean [SD] age, 62.4 [9.4] years; 25 334 female [35.9%]). Mean (SD) baseline hemoglobin was 13.6 (1.5) g/dL; baseline hematocrit was 41.5% (4.9). Seventy-eight clinical trials (67 208 participants) compared SGLT2 inhibitors with placebo, and 7 clinical trials (3335 participants) used active comparators, most commonly sitagliptin (2 trials [1158 participants]). From baseline to follow-up, hemoglobin changed by 0.55 g/dL (95% CI, 0.49 to 0.61 g/dL; P < .001) in the SGLT2 inhibitor group, and -0.08 g/dL (95% CI, -0.13 to -0.03 g/dL; P = .003) in the control group (difference, 0.60 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.55 to 0.66 g/dL; P < .001). From baseline to follow-up, hematocrit changed by 2.17% (95% CI, 1.95% to 2.39%; P < .001) in the SGLT2 inhibitor group and -0.13% (95% CI, -0.28% to 0.01%; P = .07) in the control group (difference, 2.36%; 95% CI, 2.19% to 2.52%; P < .001). Of the 6 secondary outcomes, 4 showed significant associations with SGLT2 inhibitors, including increased EPO (2.35 mIU/mL in SGLT2 inhibitor group vs 0.04 mIU/mL in control group; difference, 2.11 mIU/mL [95% CI, 0.5-3.71 mIU/mL]; P = .01) and decreased transferrin saturation (-2.2% in SGLT2 inhibitor group vs -0.10% in control group; difference, -0.84% [95% CI, -1.21% to -0.47%]; P < .001). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials, compared with control, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with small statistically significant increases in hemoglobin and hematocrit levels. The clinical significance of these findings is unclear.

title: Effect of Obicetrapib on Glycaemia and New-Onset Diabetes: Pooled Analysis of BROADWAY/BROOKLYN and an Updated Meta-analysis of CETP Inhibitor Trials
abstract: AIMS: New-onset diabetes (NoD) is a recognised effect of statin therapy potentially influencing acceptance of intensive LDL-C-lowering. In contrast, cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibition has been associated with lower NoD risk in earlier trials. We assessed the effect of the highly selective CETP inhibitor obicetrapib on glycaemia and NoD, contextualised within an updated meta-analysis of CETP inhibitor trials. METHODS: Individual participant data from the phase 3 BROADWAY and BROOKLYN trials were pooled across 1,700 participants without diabetes at baseline (899 normoglycaemic, 801 prediabetes; 38.8% women), randomised 2:1 to obicetrapib 10 mg or placebo for 52 weeks. The PRISMA-compliant, PROSPERO-registered systematic review identified six eligible trials reporting NoD. Pooled risk ratios were calculated using Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect models, with prespecified subgroup analyses by baseline glycaemic status and CETPi potency, and trial-level meta-regression. RESULTS: Obicetrapib did not increase HbA1c at week 52 vs placebo (LSMD -0.02%, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.00). NoD occurred in 6.4% (obicetrapib) versus 8.5% (placebo) (adjusted OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.47-1.03), directionally consistent across glycaemic strata. Restricted cubic spline analyses identified associations between HDL-C, apoA1 and Lp(a) changes and NoD risk, but not HbA1c change. In the meta-analysis, CETP inhibition was associated with a 16% lower risk of NoD (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.79-0.90; I2 = 0%). CONCLUSIONS: Obicetrapib did not adversely affect glycaemia and was associated with a numerically lower risk of NoD, consistent with a CETP inhibitor class signal of a modestly lower risk. The PREVAIL trial will provide larger-longer evidence about obicetrapib and NoD.

title: Physical Activity and Cardiovascular Risk in Type 2 Diabetes With Normal Body Mass Index and Abdominal Obesity: A Nationwide Cohort Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The prognostic implications of abdominal obesity and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) in patients with type 2 diabetes who have a normal body mass index remain unclear. METHODS: This nationwide retrospective cohort study included 323 029 adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes and a normal body mass index (<23 kg/m2) between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2023, from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. Abdominal obesity was defined using sex-specific waist circumference thresholds (≥90 cm for men, ≥80 cm for women). MVPA was assessed through standardized self-reported questionnaires administered during routine health screenings. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events, defined as a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure. RESULTS: Among the study population, 34 033 (10.5%) had abdominal obesity. During a median follow-up of 6.0 years (interquartile range, 2.6-9.0 years), abdominal obesity was associated with a higher risk of major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.13 [95% CI, 1.09-1.17]). Among patients with abdominal obesity, regular MVPA after diagnosis (27.1%) was associated with a significantly lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (adjusted HR 0.74 [95% CI, 0.68-0.80]), all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.72 [95% CI, 0.65-0.80]), ischemic stroke (adjusted HR 0.77 [95% CI, 0.66-0.89]), and hospitalization for heart failure (adjusted HR 0.75 [95% CI, 0.60-0.93]). The cardiovascular protective effects of MVPA were consistent regardless of statin or antidiabetic medication use. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with type 2 diabetes and a normal body mass index, abdominal obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events. Regular engagement in MVPA showed consistent cardiovascular benefits in this population, irrespective of pharmacotherapy. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT07071545.

title: Contemporary Burden, Drivers, and Risk-Factor Control Gaps Across Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Stages in US Adults, 2021 to 2023
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome staging integrates adiposity, metabolic dysfunction, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease. Contemporary national estimates of CKM stage distribution, stage drivers, and treatment gaps are needed to inform implementation of the CKM framework. METHODS: We analyzed adults aged ≥20 years in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2021 to 2023 fasting subsample. CKM stage was assigned hierarchically using American Heart Association CKM staging criteria. We estimated survey-weighted CKM stage prevalence, national population counts, stage-specific drivers, and risk-factor control and treatment gaps across stages 2 through 4. RESULTS: The analytic sample included 2958 adults, representing 245.2 million US adults. Overall, 26.4 million adults (10.8%) were stage 0, 56.8 million (23.2%) stage 1, 125.9 million (51.3%) stage 2, 13.4 million (5.5%) stage 3, and 22.7 million (9.3%) stage 4. Stage ≥1 was present in 89.2%, stage ≥2 in 66.1%, and advanced CKM (stages 3-4) in 14.7%. Among stage 1 adults, 85.1% had adiposity and 49.2% had prediabetes. Among adults with stage 2 CKM, hypertension (72.0%), metabolic syndrome (56.1%), and hypertriglyceridemia (41.9%) were common drivers. Among adults with stage 3 CKM, 95.8% met the Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events 10-year cardiovascular disease risk criterion. Risk-factor control and treatment gaps were common across stages 2 through 4, including blood pressure ≥130/80 mm Hg in 50.3% to 66.9%, lipid-lowering therapy nonuse among eligible adults in 30.1% to 59.2%, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol above the target in 64.5% to 73.9%. CONCLUSIONS: CKM syndrome affects most US adults, with stage-specific drivers and persistent risk-factor control and treatment gaps. These findings provide contemporary benchmarks for CKM surveillance and implementation.

title: Lipoprotein(a) and Risk Stratification for Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease Across the Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Continuum
abstract: BACKGROUND: Lp(a) (lipoprotein(a)) is an established risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), but its prognostic relevance across the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) continuum remains uncertain. We examined whether Lp(a) was associated with incident ASCVD across CKM stages and whether it provided complementary risk stratification beyond CKM staging. METHODS: We included 333 321 UK Biobank participants free of clinical cardiovascular disease at baseline and classified them into CKM stages 0 to 3. Elevated Lp(a) was defined as ≥125 nmol/L. The primary outcome was incident ASCVD, defined as coronary artery disease or ischemic stroke. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs), and 10-year absolute risks were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods. RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 15.3 years, 17 581 incident ASCVD events occurred. After adjustment for demographic characteristics, socioeconomic factors, lifestyle factors, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, medications, and CKM stage, elevated Lp(a) was associated with higher ASCVD risk (HR, 1.31 [95% CI, 1.25-1.36]). In joint analyses, risk increased progressively across combined CKM-Lp(a) categories, with the highest risk observed in participants with CKM stage 3 and elevated Lp(a) versus CKM stage 0 and lower Lp(a) (HR, 3.43 [95% CI, 2.74-4.31]). Ten-year ASCVD risk ranged from 0.64% to 16.30%, and the absolute risk difference associated with elevated Lp(a) increased from 0.23% in stage 0 to 2.20% in stage 3. CONCLUSIONS: Elevated Lp(a) was associated with higher incident ASCVD risk across the CKM continuum. Although relative associations were broadly consistent across CKM stages, absolute risk increments associated with elevated Lp(a) were greater at more advanced CKM stages, supporting the integration of Lp(a) into CKM-based risk stratification for primary prevention.

title: Familial hypercholesterolaemia and thymic ageing in a Chinese cohort
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Lifelong exposure to elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) patients not only increases the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, but also affects other organs beyond the cardiovascular system. In a large FH cohort, this study investigated the effects of hypercholesterolaemia on the thymic output and explored whether lipid-lowering therapy can reverse these effects. METHODS: According to the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria, 562 heterozygous FH patients (236 treatment-naïve, 326 on lipid-lowering therapy) and 295 age-matched healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. Thymic output was measured by circulating CD4+ recent thymic emigrants (RTEs) with flow cytometry, and T-cell receptor excision circles in sorted naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Repertoire diversity and clonal expansion were evaluated by T-cell receptor beta sequencing. RESULTS: Compared with HCs, treatment-naïve FH patients displayed a significantly reduced percentage of CD4+ RTE among naïve CD4+ T cells, particularly in those aged 18-30 years or carrying highly pathogenic LDLR variants. T-cell receptor excision circle analysis supported reduced thymic output in both CD4+ and CD8+ naïve T cells. Quantified thymic ageing further showed that FH patients reached the median CD4+ RTE percentage of HCs ∼6 years earlier (males: 19.12 vs 25.51 years; females: 19.18 vs 25.58 years). Consistent with reduced thymic output, FH patients showed skewing towards high-frequency T-cell receptor beta clones. Statin-treated FH patients, particularly females, showed higher circulating CD4+ RTE levels than statin-naïve FH patients. CONCLUSIONS: Hypercholesterolaemia was associated with reduced thymic output, while statin-treated patients showed partially preserved circulating CD4+ RTE levels, supporting integrated metabolic and immunologic strategies for FH management.

title: ICare-FASTER (Improving Care by Faster Risk Stratification Through Use of High-Sensitivity Point-of-Care Troponin in Patients Presenting With Possible Acute Coronary Syndrome in the Emergency Department): A Stepped-Wedge Cluster-Randomized Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Point-of-care high-sensitivity cTn (cardiac troponin; hs-cTn) testing has the potential to expedite decision-making and reduce emergency department (ED) length of stay for patients presenting with possible myocardial infarction by ensuring that results are consistently available when sought by clinicians. We assessed the real-life effectiveness and safety of implementing point-of-care hs-cTn testing in the ED. METHODS: We conducted a pragmatic, stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial. The control arm was usual care with an accelerated diagnostic pathway using a single-sample rule-out step with a central laboratory hs-cTn assay. The intervention arm used the same pathway with a point-of-care hs-cTnI assay. The primary effectiveness outcome was ED length of stay assessed using a generalized linear mixed model. The safety outcome was myocardial infarction or cardiac death within 30 days. RESULTS: Six sites participated, with 59 980 ED presentations (44 747 individuals; mean 61±19 years of age; 49.5% female) from February 2023 through January 2025; 31 392 presentations were during the intervention arm. After adjustment for covariates associated with length of stay, the intervention reduced length of stay by 13% (95% CI, 9%-16%; P<0.001), corresponding to a reduction of 47 minutes (95% CI, 33-61 minutes) from a mean length of stay in the control arm of 376 minutes. The 30-day myocardial infarction or cardiac death rate was similar in the control and intervention arms (0.39% and 0.39%, respectively; P=0.54). CONCLUSIONS: Implementation of whole-blood hs-cTnI testing at the point of care into an accelerated diagnostic pathway was safe and reduced length of stay in the ED compared with laboratory testing. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.anzctr.org.au; Unique identifier: ACTRN12619001189112.

title: Immediate Complete Revascularization During Index Admission in Older Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction
abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether age affects the comparative treatment effect of immediate complete revascularization (CR) vs staged CR during the index admission in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and multivessel disease remains unknown. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to assess how age influences clinical outcomes in patients with with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and multivessel disease randomized to immediate or in-hospital staged CR. METHODS: This is a secondary analysis of the OPTION-STEMI (Optimal Timing of Fractional Flow Reserve-Guided Complete Revascularization for Non-Infarct-Related Artery in ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction with Multivessel Disease) trial, which included 994 patients randomized to immediate or in-hospital staged CR. The primary endpoint at 1 year, defined as a composite of all-cause death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or any unplanned revascularization, was analyzed according to age and CR strategy. RESULTS: A significant interaction was found between age, as a continuous variable, and CR strategy for the primary endpoint (interaction P = 0.015). The HR for the primary endpoint was initially higher in the staged CR arm until approximately 67 years, after which it increased steadily in the immediate CR arm. In the binary analysis, a significantly higher incidence of the primary endpoint was observed in the immediate CR arm compared with the staged CR arm in patients ≥70 years (45 of 202 [22.3%] vs 29 of 210 [13.8%]; HR: 1.68; 95% CI: 1.06-2.69; log-rank P = 0.029), but not in patients <70 years (20 of 296 [6.8%] vs 24 of 286 [8.4%]; HR: 0.80; 95% CI: 0.45-1.45; log-rank P = 0.470) (multiplicative interaction P = 0.054; relative excess risk due to interaction P = 0.016). CONCLUSIONS: This post hoc analysis of the OPTION-STEMI trial demonstrates that older patients experience significantly worse clinical outcomes with immediate CR than with in-hospital staged CR. These findings suggest that age modifies the treatment effect of the CR strategy and warrant confirmation in adequately powered trials (Timing of FFR-guided PCI for Non-IRA in STEMI and MVD [OPTION-STEMI]; NCT04626882).

title: Radiation Vasculopathy of the Coronary Arteries: State-of-the Art Review
abstract: Radiation-associated coronary artery disease (RACAD) is a distinct form of coronary artery disease with several specific biological and clinical aspects as well as key knowledge gaps. RACAD is prevalent in patients with cardiac exposure to radiotherapy. As radiotherapy is integral to the effective treatment of many thoracic malignancies, improved long-term survivorship is coupled with increased risk for RACAD. Ionizing radiation induces free radical generation and activation of proinflammatory cascades, leading to endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis. Risks for RACAD are determined both by radiotherapy, including the radiation dose and the proximity of coronary arteries to the radiotherapy field, and by patient-specific factors, such as younger age, higher baseline cardiovascular risk, and concurrent cardiotoxic systemic therapies. Importantly, radiotherapy delivery is highly individualized on the basis of tumor location and treatment strategy, resulting in heterogeneous coronary exposure to radiation and patient-to-patient variability. Clinical presentation may occur early, within 1 to 2 years, especially in patients with higher cardiac radiation doses (eg, lung or esophageal cancer), or after a latency period of 5 to 20 years with lower cardiac dose radiation exposure (eg, left-sided breast cancer). Patients generally present with symptoms similar to conventional coronary artery disease. However, RACAD symptoms may be underrecognized in cancer survivors due to overlapping treatment-related fatigue, pulmonary disease, or competing oncologic symptoms. Diagnosis and management generally follow standard coronary artery disease guidelines while incorporating cancer-specific considerations, such as planned oncologic surgeries, bleeding risk, postradiotherapy complications such as atretic internal mammary arteries, and cardiotoxic effects of systemic cancer therapies. Primary prevention of RACAD is critical, emphasizing advances in precision radiotherapy, including delivery techniques with improved coronary dosimetry, and cardiac shielding. Key knowledge gaps include understanding long-term outcomes with contemporary 3-dimensional conformal radiotherapy techniques, validated cancer-specific risk prediction models on the basis of coronary dosimetry, optimal surveillance protocols, targeted molecular pharmacotherapies, and risk analysis of percutaneous versus surgical management of RACAD. Prospective studies are needed to develop cancer- and dosimetry-specific risk calculators, validating cardioprotective interventions, and improving multidisciplinary cardio-oncology collaboration to optimize early detection of RACAD and timely intervention in the growing population of cancer survivors.

title: Effectiveness of digital health interventions for care integration in coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: AIM: To assess the effectiveness of digital health interventions (DHIs) supporting care integration for coronary artery disease (CAD) in improving health outcomes compared to usual care. METHODS: For this systematic review, we searched MEDLINE, CINAHL, EBSCO Psychology and Behavioural Sciences Collection, Scopus, and Web of Science from 1 January 1995 to 5 November 2025. We included studies reporting primary data on DHIs supporting care integration for patients with CAD. Primary endpoints were all-cause mortality and readmissions, and CVD events. Secondary endpoints were the control of cardiovascular risk factors. We conducted random-effects meta-analyses in RevMan and assessed risk of bias with Cochrane's RoB tools. RESULTS: We included 72 studies (23,111 participants), assessing 45 in the meta-analysis. All DHIs supported person-centred care integration (n=72) while few DHIs addressed clinical care integration (n=22), professional integration (n=12) and functional integration (n=22). Compared to usual care, DHIs supporting care integration had significant reductions in the odds of CVD events (OR: 0.74 [0.59, 0.92], df=5, p=0.02), but not in all-cause mortality or readmissions. CONCLUSIONS: Although this review shows that DHIs supporting care integration were associated with reduced CVD events compared to usual care, the current evidence remains concentrated primarily on person-centred care integration, with limited studies evaluating broader dimensions of care integration at organisational and systemic levels. These findings highlight the important evidence gaps of DHIs in supporting more comprehensive and system-level integration in cardiovascular care. Further research is necessary to understand the influence of DHI modality and function on effectiveness of care integration.

title: Acute heart failure in emergency settings
abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) represents a major cause of emergency medical care worldwide and continues to carry a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality despite advances in chronic heart failure management. Most patients with AHF present to emergency departments (EDs), where the first hours of care are critical to determine prognosis. Of these, some have been previously evaluated and treated by prehospital emergency medical services before ED arrival. This consensus document summarizes the current evidence and provides practical advice to emergency physicians for the diagnosis, treatment, and disposition of patients with AHF in these emergency settings (emergency medical services and ED). It emphasizes the importance of a rapid phenotypic classification into acute decompensated heart failure, acute pulmonary oedema, isolated right ventricular failure, or cardiogenic shock, as a key tool to guide early management and triage decisions. It reviews evidence on prehospital and ED management, including the use of biomarkers, imaging, ventilatory support, diuretic and vasodilator strategies, and early initiation or continuation of guideline-directed medical therapy. It also discusses risk stratification and disposition decisions supported by validated tools. Finally, it identifies major knowledge gaps and future research priorities, including pragmatic trials to assess prehospital interventions, biomarker-guided therapy, and early initiation of disease-modifying treatments. Ultimately, this consensus document is aimed to contribute to the improvement of outcomes in AHF.

title: Management of Heart transplant recipients for the non Heart Transplant health care provider. A Clinical Consensus Statement of the Heart Failure Association (HFA) and the Association of Cardiovascular Nursing & Allied Professions (ACNAP) of the ESC
abstract: Heart transplantation (HTx) remains the gold standard treatment for selected patients with advanced heart failure and survival after transplantation has substantially improved over recent decades. As a consequence, the number of long-term HTx recipients continues to increase, and these patients are now frequently encountered in routine practice outside specialized transplant centers. Their management remains complex due to the use of chronic immunosuppression, transplant-specific complications, and a growing burden of comorbidities in the perspective of increasing longevity. Non-transplant cardiologists, general practitioners, and other healthcare professionals are therefore increasingly involved in their care but often have limited experience of post-transplant management. This clinical consensus statement from the Heart Failure Association (HFA) and the Association of Cardiovascular Nursing & Allied Professions (ACNAP) of the ESC provides practical support and a structured framework for healthcare providers involved in the care of HTx recipients outside dedicated transplant centers. The document reviews key aspects of post-transplant management, including outlining principles of care according to time from transplantation, essential knowledge around immunosuppressive therapy and drug monitoring, recognition and initial management of rejection, infection prophylaxis and treatment, and surveillance of long-term complications such as cardiac allograft vasculopathy, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, and metabolic disorders. In addition, specific clinical situations frequently encountered in practice-including fertility and pregnancy, non-cardiac surgery, rehabilitation, and palliative care-are discussed. Particular emphasis is placed on the organization of shared-care models between transplant centers and community providers and on identifying clinical scenarios requiring early referral. Through providing practical recommendations and a structured framework for follow-up, this document aims to support non-specialist clinicians in the safe management of HTx recipients and to facilitate timely collaboration with transplant centers.

title: Individualized Cardiac Index-Guided Hemodynamic Therapy in High-Risk Patients Undergoing Elective Major Abdominal Surgery: The PELICAN Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: IMPORTANCE: It remains unclear if intraoperative hemodynamic therapy should be guided by cardiac index. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy vs routine hemodynamic therapy improves outcomes in high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This multicenter, single-blind, superiority randomized clinical trial enrolled high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery between October 8, 2023, and October 25, 2025, at 12 university medical centers in Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, and Spain. The date of last follow-up was January 15, 2026. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized to individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index vs routine hemodynamic therapy (with blinded cardiac index monitoring). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was a composite of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days. RESULTS: Of the 1128 patients enrolled, 1111 were randomized and 1095 were included in the primary analysis (median age, 67 years [IQR, 59-74 years]; 49.4% were female). The primary outcome occurred in 243 of 549 patients (44.3%) in the individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy group vs 256 of 546 patients (46.9%) in the routine hemodynamic therapy group (relative risk, 0.94 [95.1% CI, 0.83-1.08]; P = .38). There were no between-group differences for the incidence of the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, individualized cardiac index-guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient's preoperative resting cardiac index did not reduce the incidence of a composite outcome of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days compared with routine hemodynamic therapy. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05648279.

title: Dose-Response Associations of Exercise Modalities With Cardiorespiratory Fitness in Heart Failure: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis
abstract: AIMS: Exercise training improves cardiorespiratory fitness in patients with heart failure, yet the dose-response relationship across different exercise modalities remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different exercise modalities and their standardized doses on peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) in patients with heart failure. METHODS: We systematically searched multiple databases from inception through March 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing exercise interventions with controls. Exercise modalities were categorized as interval aerobic training (IAT), continuous aerobic training (CAT), resistance training (RT), mind-body training (MBT), and their combinations. Exercise dose was uniformly quantified as weekly metabolic equivalents (MET-min/week). A Bayesian model-based network dose-response meta-analysis was performed. RESULTS: A total of 100 trials involving 5,353 patients were included. The dose-response relationship followed an Emax curve, with ED50 values clustering around 80-90 MET-min/week. A weekly dose of 500 MET-min yielded considerable benefit, and 750-1000 MET-min approached maximal benefit for nearly all modalities. The top three ranked interventions were IAT (Emax = 3.50, 95% CrI: 2.49-4.60), RT (Emax = 3.66, 95% CrI: 1.96-5.85), and IAT+RT (Emax = 3.49, 95% CrI: 1.26-5.79). CONCLUSIONS: The exercise dose-response relationship in heart failure follows an Emax curve, with distinct dose-benefit profiles across different exercise modalities. Based on the current evidence, the following preliminary considerations may be offered: for patients with limited exercise tolerance, MBT may be considered as one of the preferred options; for those with moderate exercise tolerance, IAT+RT or CAT+RT may be suitable choices; for patients with good exercise tolerance, IAT or RT may be considered; and for patients with comorbid obesity, CAT may be incorporated into a comprehensive management program.

title: Cardiac Structure and Function in Women After Preeclampsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Preeclampsia increases the risk of long-term heart failure (HF) by 4-fold. Unfortunately, however, universal guidelines for postpartum HF surveillance are lacking. Stage B/subclinical HF has been shown to predict risk of major adverse cardiac outcomes. Some suggest that initiating cardioprotective therapy at this early stage can reduce progression to symptomatic HF. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this review was to explore cardiac structure and function in women with a history of preeclampsia and to identify when subclinical HF develops in this group. METHODS: A systematic search of MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL was conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines to identify all studies assessing left ventricular function on transthoracic echocardiography in women with a history of preeclampsia. RESULTS: A total of 45 case-control studies comprising 8,991 women, including 2,288 women with a history of preeclampsia, were included in the final analysis. During pregnancy, women with preeclampsia had a higher left ventricular mass index (LVMI) (standard mean difference: 10.85 [95% CI: 6.30-15.39]), relative wall thickness (0.05 [95% CI: 0.03-0.08]), E/e' (1.58 [95% CI: 1.02-2.13]), isovolumetric relaxation time (8.74 [95% CI: 3.14-14.34]), lower E/A ratio (-0.27 [95% CI: -0.51 to -0.04]) and reduced absolute global longitudinal strain (GLS) values (2.27 [95% CI: 0.43-4.11]), indicating reduced myocardial function compared with normotensive controls. Postpartum, GLS remained reduced, and LVMI remained elevated in women with a history of preeclampsia. This difference persisted out to 10 years postpartum. There was no significant difference in all other variables >6 months postpartum. Evidence for persistent LVMI elevation >6 months postpartum was not robust in sensitivity analyses excluding overlapping cohorts. Left ventricular ejection fraction and right ventricular function remained similar in the preeclampsia and control groups throughout. CONCLUSIONS: Preeclampsia is associated with subclinical myocardial dysfunction, characterized by impaired GLS and increased LVMI. Persistent impairment in GLS was observed up to 10 years postpartum, whereas the association with elevated LVMI beyond 6 months postpartum should be interpreted with caution. Further studies are required to assess when subclinical myocardial dysfunction progresses to symptomatic clinical HF.

title: A Common CD36 Variant and the Genetic Landscape of Dilated Cardiomyopathy in Individuals of African Ancestry
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure that disproportionately affects individuals of predominantly African ancestry, among whom familial clustering of disease is more pronounced relative to those of predominantly European ancestry. Truncating variants in TTN, which encodes the sarcomeric protein titin, are the most common established monogenic cause of DCM. A common CD36 nonsense variant enriched among individuals of African ancestry has also been shown to account for a substantial burden of DCM. OBJECTIVE: To compare the contribution of a CD36 nonsense variant to DCM risk with that of truncating variants in TTN and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other established genes for DCM. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Multicohort genetic association study including participants of African and European ancestry with exome or genome sequence data and DCM case status from the following 4 US datasets: All of Us Research Program (recruitment: 2017-present; last follow-up: August 27, 2024), Million Veteran Program (recruitment: 2011-present; last follow-up: September 30, 2024), Penn Medicine Biobank (recruitment: 2013-present; last follow-up: November 14, 2022), and the DCM Precision Medicine Study (recruitment: 2016-2020; last follow-up: March 15, 2020). EXPOSURE: Carrier status for TTN truncating variants, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 11 high-confidence genes for DCM, and the nonsense variant CD36 Y325* (0, 1, or 2 copies). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Risk of DCM, prevalence of variant carriers among DCM cases, and population attributable fraction of DCM. RESULTS: Among 82 623 individuals of predominantly African ancestry across 4 cohorts, the mean age was 53.4 years (SD, 13.9 years), 47 124 were male, and 1316 had DCM. Individuals who were homozygous for the CD36 Y325* risk allele had a higher risk of DCM (odds ratio [OR], 4.8; 95% CI, 3.1-7.3) as did those who were heterozygous (OR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2-1.7). TTN truncating variants also conferred an elevated risk of DCM in participants of African ancestry (OR, 8.5; 95% CI, 5.5-13.0). Among 1316 individuals of African ancestry classified as DCM cases, 33 (2.5%) were homozygous for CD36, 56 (4.3%) had TTN truncating variants, and 16 (1.2%) had pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other high-confidence genes for DCM. In population-level analyses incorporating both heterozygous and homozygous CD36 Y325* carriers, the population attributable fraction for CD36 (9.0% [6.2% for heterozygous carriers and 2.8% for homozygous carriers]) surpassed the population attributable fraction for TTN truncating variants (3.7%). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In 4 US cohorts, an ancestry-specific CD36 variant contributed more to DCM burden among individuals of African ancestry than established genes for DCM, including TTN truncating variants that are typically considered the most common genetic cause. These findings reshape the known genetic architecture of DCM in individuals of African ancestry and highlight the importance of representation in genomic research.

title: Long-Term Outcome of Myectomy Associated With Secondary Mitral Valve Chordal Cutting in Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: BACKGROUND: The recent introduction of cardiac myosin inhibitors has modified the therapy of left ventricular outflow obstruction in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and is raising uncertainties regarding the future role of surgery in the management of obstructive HCM. However, it is likely that a proportion of patients will continue to present with advanced, highly symptomatic HCM, despite medical therapy, and require surgical intervention. We previously reported the short-term results of cutting anterior mitral leaflet secondary chordae in combination with septal myectomy in patients with obstructive HCM. This operative approach has shown excellent results in several short-term studies from our and other centers. However, no data are currently available regarding the long-term outcome of this novel surgical procedure. OBJECTIVES: The study sought to investigate the long-term results of myectomy associated with chordal cutting. METHODS: Long-term results were assessed in 350 consecutive patients with obstructive HCM who underwent this operation at our center over a 5-year period. Median follow-up was 5.6 years (Q1-Q3: 4.2-6.3 years). RESULTS: Including 2 in-hospital deaths (surgical mortality 0.6%), 6-year overall survival after surgery was 96% and did not differ from that of the general Italian population matched for age and sex (P = 0.331). Follow-up information was available in 344 (99%) patients. At the most recent evaluation, 271 (79%) patients were asymptomatic in NYHA functional class I, 65 (19%) were in NYHA functional class II, and 8 (2%) were in NYHA functional class III. During follow-up, there were 14 deaths, 6 of which were unrelated to HCM. At most recent echocardiographic evaluation, ≥95% of patients had no residual left ventricular outflow gradient, clinically significant mitral regurgitation, or impaired systolic function. CONCLUSIONS: Our results show that cutting thickened and/or retracted secondary chordae of the anterior mitral leaflet in association with septal myectomy has excellent long-term clinical and hemodynamic results in patients with obstructive HCM. These findings may further increase the number of myectomy referral centers and the availability of the surgical option for severely symptomatic HCM patients unresponsive to medical treatment.
